Q: PermissionError(13, 'A device attached to the system is not functioning.', None, 31)Serial port COM4 A:

I encountered the same issue, and my way to fix is to install the older version of CH340 driver, the version from 2011 specifically.

Detail about my case:

- I'm using ESP8266 nodemcu 12E with CH340 UART on board, can't flash and monitor via vscode, also can't flash via ESP's original flash download tool.

- But I have other ESP32 and ESP8266 boards with same UART and works just fine.

- I found out that the faulty board has the UART chip name erased, and that my other CH340 UART USBs (that name erased too) also have the same problem flashing ESP01 board (same ESP8266).

- So I think the problem came from the fake or bad quality UART chips that name erased, maybe they work fine until some recent updates, from both OS and driver, so the latest CH340 driver of 2024 just can't connect to those.

Conclusion:

- Switch back to 2011 version of CH340 driver, uninstall the newer ones, and use them temporarily, I haven't seen any problem with this old one so far.

- Buy the good boards, you see my 2 boards still work fine with latest driver, only fail with the annonymous UART chips.

Glad if I can help anyone, took me a day to figure out. ^^

Q: The term '' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet, function, script file A:

How are you running your program? When I write a program with your exact code, it works.

You have written a command line script in Dart and thus need to run it as such. For example, if you saved your program in the file my_app.dart, then from the command line you could run dart my_app.dart and it'll run your script.

Another way to run it is to create a dart console app and run it using dart run as outlined here: https://dart.dev/tutorials/server/get-started. This would be my recommendation and if you follow the guide I think you'll be able to figure it out, but to quickly confirm your code works you can do the first suggestion.

Q: Grant CREATE/ALTER permission to user A:

you try below way

Create a Role

    CREATE ROLE [user_dev] AUTHORIZATION db_securityadmin;
    GO



    GRANT CREATE PROCEDURE TO [user_dev];
    GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, ALTER, EXECUTE, VIEW DEFINITION ON SCHEMA::dbo TO [user_dev]

Create user and login for test and add to the user_dev role

    CREATE LOGIN test WITH PASSWORD = 'dfgdfg' 
    CREATE USER test 
    EXEC sp_addrolemember @rolename = 'user_dev', @membername = 'test';
    GO

Then create a trigger to restrict user_dev role from creating table and drop

    CREATE TRIGGER tr_db_DenyDropAlterTable
    ON DATABASE 
    FOR DROP_TABLE, ALTER_TABLE 
    AS 
    BEGIN 
       IF IS_MEMBER('user_dev') = 1 
       BEGIN 
           PRINT 'Not allowed'; 
           ROLLBACK TRAN; 
       END; 
    END; 
    GO

Q: How to create password protected tar archive with custom filename in Windows/Linux? A:

This might be the most glaring example I've ever seen of the Dunning Kruger effect on this site, but let's go over some very basic ideas you're misunderstanding, specifically about archives.

  • tar doesn't offer compression since the Unix philosophy says that's jobs of other tools. While most versions of tar can pipe directly into the common compression tools (e.g., tar czf) it's not required. This means that if a new compression algorithm comes out and it plays nicely with other Unix tools, I can do something like tar cf - my-folder | super-compression-tool > my-folder.tar.sct.
  • Encryption works the exact same way. If I want to encrypt using openssl, I can do that just fine. If I want to encrypt using gnutls, same deal. If I want to use a proprietary encryption tool, it's all the same. This also means that the metadata about my archive is encrypted, which can help hinder an attacker. rar and 7z (I think) let you encrypt some of the metadata when you add files, but not all of it (and as far as I know, you cannot encrypt any metadata with zip).
  • Whether a filesystem is self-healing, encrypted, and backed up have nothing to do with archive tools. The machine I'm typing this on uses full disk encryption using dm-crypt and conforms to Department of Defense standards. The decrypted filesystem is ext4, but I could just as easily have used any filesystem my kernel supports. Outside my initramfs and /etc/fstab, nothing on my system cares in the least about the disk encryption (and the latter is only because I use mapped mount points). Again, this is basic separation of duties that's common in any Unix-like system.
  • If you're referring to data integrity of archives themselves, this is not their problem (again). We already have hashing, and most packages provide hash values of their releases. I'm running Gentoo (which uses tar.xz for package distribution) and it validates hashes as archives are downloaded. You can use any hash algorithm you fancy, including the full suite from openssl and similar.
  • Simplicity is usually better. Note that by keeping tar simple and separating concerns like data integrity, compression, and encryption, it's trivial to update on the fly. If somebody breaks AES-128 tomorrow, nobody has to change a single line of tar's source code to regain data security. Is the same true if zip's encryption is broken? The same holds if there's a flaw or vulnerability in compression tooling as xz came dangerously close to suffering.

You're clearly passionate about technology and security, so think through some of these issues you have with existing tooling. And remember that any solution you propose has to 1) be better than what already exists and 2) be sufficiently better that it's worth the cost of migration. The latter is important as tar has decades of use, so your solution is going to have to justify changing automated pipeliens, API endpoints, and so on.
